Halley: A Predictive Control Plane for Optical AI
Data Center Networks
Manav Mishra1 and Krishna M. Sivalingam2
1Prompeteer.ai, Los Angeles, CA 90066, USA
2Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai, India
Emails: manav@prompeteer.com, skrishnam@cse.iitm.ac.in
CORRESPONDING AUTHOR: Manav Mishra.
Abstract—A frontier AI model is trained in an AI data center,
on tens of thousands of accelerators joined by a dedicated network,
and every training step ends with all of them exchanging data at
once. Between racks, that network is optical, and each of its four
layers, from lasers to switches, runs a fixed or after-the-fact policy.
Lasers sharing an enclosure, cooling, and power can fail together.
At a fixed spare ratio, correlated failure provably caps a pool’s
availability however large it grows. In this paper, we present a
comprehensive predictive control plane framework, called Halley,
that reads each resource’s next state and acts before the failure
occurs. It has four components, each carrying a formal guarantee:
LightReserve that sizes the laser pool to provide a coverage
bound, FoldFit that schedules the switch within 11/9 of the
optimal, ThermaLead that holds a microring with one-step-ahead
control, and TriageGuard that protects the highest-risk modules
first. Halley gives each layer a predictive controller that defers to
the deployed policy when unsure. Composed from simulations at
that point, effective goodput, the share of ideal throughput kept,
rises from 65.2% to 76.5% if a window that exhausts its spares
is lost. If only the dark channels’ bandwidth is lost, it reaches
67.4%. Per megawatt, that is up to 1.03–1.17 times the training;
for the same training, up to 3.3–14.7% less data center capacity.
Halley’s fallback circuits are formally verified and are shown to
achieve close timing on a commercial FPGA, and pass a 130 nm
signoff.
Index Terms—Co-packaged optics, common-cause failure, data
center networks, distributed training, microring modulators,
optical circuit switching, optical interconnects, predictive control,
reliability
I. INTRODUCTION
A frontier AI training run usually occupies a single cluster
in an AI data center, where a dedicated network moves data
among tens of thousands of accelerators. Between racks, copper
cannot carry that data within its power and reach budget, so
the network is optical [1], and the industry is now moving the
optics onto the package itself, next to the switch or accelerator
silicon, an arrangement known as co-packaged optics (CPO).
This network, the fabric, has an optical data plane of four
layers, each managed on its own today. A shared pool of
external lasers supplies light to many photonic engines, the
on-package optical transceivers of CPO. An optical circuit
switch (OCS) joins those engines to one another by connecting
whole light paths instead of forwarding individual packets.
Microring modulators, ring resonators a few microns in radius,
encode the data onto each wavelength. The lasers arrive in
field-replaceable modules that are swapped in service.
At hundred-thousand-accelerator scale, reliability, network
topology, and checkpointing have become first-order design
constraints [1]. Each layer faces an online allocation decision
under a hard service constraint: how many spare lasers the
pool should hold, which circuits the switch should hold and for
how long, where each ring’s heater should be set, and which
modules receive the few hot spares, each wired to its module in
advance. The deployed policies this paper replaces, which we
call reactive for short, either fix each answer once in advance or
make it only after the event it should have anticipated. Training
is bulk-synchronous: every training step ends in a collective,
a phase in which all accelerators communicate at once and
which also acts as a barrier, so the step finishes only when
its slowest link does. A drifted ring, a failed laser, or a late
switch reconfiguration therefore leaves every accelerator idle
at that barrier.
Software-defined networking provisioned for a separate
control plane from the data plane. Production optical fabrics use
that approach for provisioning. For example, Google’s Jupiter
fabric routes on a predicted traffic matrix [2] and TPUv4 recon-
figures its optical circuit switches to ride through outages [3],
[4]. Similarly, Ironwood TPU’s 9,216-chip superpods use them
to route around interruptions, the MixNet research system
reconfigures ahead of a predicted all-to-all [5]. The Opus
system reconfigures photonic rails at the boundaries between
parallelism phases [6]. Failure prediction for pluggable optical
transceivers is now validated on production data [7], [8]. We
observed that existing control planes do not forecast the co-
packaged optical hardware itself, a laser’s failure or a ring’s
drift, and hence do not act before the failure or drift arrives.
Proposed Halley framework: This work presents Halley,
a control plane that provides these necessary features. The
system has multiple components as described below. The Halley
framework provides every layer with a component of its own.
LightReserve sizes the laser pool to a coverage bound instead
of a fixed ratio: a floor on the chance that its spares absorb
every failure in a window, valid for the assumed failure rate
and correlation. FoldFit schedules the OCS so that, under
stated conditions, a schedule’s total dwell time, the time its
circuits are held, stays within 11/9 of the shortest possible, a
bound that leaves out switching delay. ThermaLead sets each
microring’s heater ahead of the drift. TriageGuard steers a
limited budget of hot spares to the modules most likely to
fail. Each component predicts its layer’s next state and acts
arXiv:2611.04408v1  [cs.NI]  3 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
2
before it arrives. Each steps aside to the reactive system that it
replaces when its forecast is stale or unsure. Hence, for such
a forecast the result is no worse than current systems, though
a confident but wrong forecast has no such floor yet.
Adding spares is the usual way to keep a shared laser
pool lit. In a co-packaged pool the lasers are unlikely to fail
independently. NVIDIA’s external laser module holds eight
lasers in one temperature-controlled enclosure [9]. Hence, the
lasers of a module share its heat and often one power supply,
and a thermal or power fault that stresses one laser stresses its
neighbors as well. Failures that arrive together can exhaust the
spares. Growing the pool at the same spare ratio, the share of
the pool held as spares, does not spread that risk away, since
the next burst of failures is correlated too.
At a fixed spare ratio, availability converges as the pool
grows to a closed-form ceiling A∗< 1 that depends on the
failure correlation ρ and the per-laser failure probability but not
on the pool’s size. Raising the spare ratio does lift availability,
but past a certain point so slowly that a high target needs a
pool larger than any operator would deploy. The limit itself is
classical. When exchangeable failures are positively correlated,
the failed fraction of a large pool converges to a random level
instead of to its mean [10]. Common-cause models in reliability
engineering bound redundant systems the same way [11], [12].
What this paper adds is its consequence for a pooled laser
supply: where the cap binds, what it costs in spares, and the
cheaper alternative. However, correlation can be controlled.
Separating the lasers into distinct thermal and power domains
and sourcing them from diverse batches raises the ceiling,
which redundancy cannot.
Technical contributions: The main contributions are:
• First, it carries the classical exchangeable limit over to
pooled laser supplies and proves that in a pool of many
modules the correlation between modules, more than
within them, sets the cap. Under a stated cost model,
it also finds that decorrelating before buying spares is the
cheaper path across the range of correlations considered
plausible.
• Second, it builds the proposed Halley control plane
framework, that has four major components. Three of
its four components carry a formal guarantee, stated in
idealized form later. The novel aspect is the design for
the failure physics of the AI data center.
• Third, it composes the components into effective cluster
goodput under two readings of a spare shortfall, couples
the laser and thermal losses through a shared common
cause, reports the tail as well as the mean, and proves a
closed form for the correlation-driven part of that tail.
• Fourth, it synthesizes, places, and routes the fallback
circuits for a commercial field-programmable gate array,
carries the same sources through signoff as a SkyWater
130 nm layout, and formally verifies their register-transfer
design, the part of Halley that can be built today.
The paper also reports a detailed performance study of the
proposed mechanisms, based on simulation and mathematical
modeling, and their circuit-level realization: an FPGA build
and a signed-off SkyWater 130 nm layout. The software
implementation of these components and the hardware design
are available at [13].
Important Results: At the correlation we assume for a well-
built package and the stress failure rate of Section III-III-B, a
pool with one spare per active laser, the 2× budget cap we
assume throughout, cannot pass 99.670% availability however
large it grows. A reserve of four spares for 32 channels, the
proportion an analyst reports for a related shipping part, reaches
only 86.3%. Availability of 99.999% is then out of reach for
any spare ratio within that cap. For a 32-channel pool at
that correlation, 99.999% stays out of reach within the 2×
cap whenever a laser’s failure probability per restock window
exceeds about 2.4 × 10−4. At 50 failures per billion hours
(50 FIT), the Optical Internetworking Forum (OIF) target for a
laser source, which we apply to each laser, a laser crosses that
probability once the restock window exceeds about 200 days.
With the spare count held at the 23 lasers our sizing rule
returns for a 99% target, cutting the correlation from ρ = 0.15
to ρ = 0.03 moves availability from about 99% to just past
99.999%. Under a stated cost model at the stress rate, reaching
99.999% by separating the pool first and then sizing its spares
costs $44,100 in all, against $234,000 for spares alone.
The overall figure of merit is effective cluster goodput,
defined as the fraction of the cluster’s ideal throughput that
survives the losses of the fabric. At the stress setting, composing
the simulated components lifts it from 65.2% to 76.5%, a 17.3%
relative gain. That figure counts every window whose failures
exhaust the spares as lost, which we call the coverage reading.
On the lit-share reading, in which only the dark channels’
bandwidth is lost, goodput rises from the same 65.2% baseline
to just 67.4%. Most of the gain thus comes from a provisioning
decision: the larger spare pool that LightReserve sizes for the
correlation a static reserve ignores. Holding that pool to the 2×
cap costs only 0.2 points, and where no spare count within the
cap reaches a target, LightReserve determines the decorrelation
it needs. ThermaLead’s simple forecast does slightly worse
than the deployed dither lock on the stress trace; gated to fall
back to that lock whenever its recent error is the larger of the
two, it has 2.1% fewer lock losses. At 50 FIT and a 90-day
restock the fixed reserve already covers nearly every window,
so the composed relative gain falls to about 1.3%; with yearly
restocks, 99.999% still exceeds the 2× cap at 50 FIT.
Within each reading, the stress-case gain is an upper bound
on the useful compute freed from the same silicon and power,
because it treats fabric stall as the only recoverable loss. This
bound matters because power and local approval now limit how
fast new AI data centers are built. A new grid connection can
take five to ten years [14]. Around 45 US data center projects
worth $68 billion were blocked or delayed at the local level
between April and June 2026 [15]. Every point of goodput that
the fabric loses is capacity that was built and powered but did
no useful work. At the bound, what Halley recovers means up
to 14.7% fewer new megawatts to site and connect for a given
training target, or up to 1.17 times as much training from the
power already in place, with no wait for a new grid connection.
On the lit-share reading the figures are 3.3% and 1.03 times.
Energy per unit of training falls too, though by less, since a
waiting accelerator draws less than full power.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II
presents the background material and related work. Section III
presents the impact of failure correlation on various metrics
such as availability. Section IV presents the control plane
framework and the four mechanisms proposed in this paper.
Section V presents a detailed performance study of the proposed
mechanisms based on simulation and mathematical modeling
studies. Section VI presents the circuit-level realization of
the proposed mechanisms, built for a commercial FPGA and
signed off as a SkyWater 130 nm layout. Section VII presents
a detailed discussion of the proposed framework including its
limitations. Section VIII concludes the paper.
II. BACKGROUND
This section presents the relevant background and related
material.
A. Data Center Networks
The fabric is kept separate from the general-purpose front-
end network, and purpose-built production fabrics such as
Alibaba’s High Performance Network (HPN) have moved far
from the classical data center architecture [16].
1) Optical Networking: Optics replaces a wiring problem
with an allocation problem at two levels: inside a single
link and across the fabric that joins the links. Inside a link,
wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) multiplies capacity
without adding cable, because each channel travels on its own
wavelength, and that makes capacity allocation a scheduling
problem: which transmitter sends on which wavelength, and
when. The problem has a long literature on star-coupled and
mesh WDM networks, covering prediction-based and interval-
based schedulers [17]–[19] and restoration mechanisms for
channel and link failures [20], [21].
The same problem recurs across the fabric in optical circuit
switching. An OCS passes the signal through untouched at
any line rate, but demand shifts, so a scheduler must break the
demand matrix, the traffic each endpoint must send to each
other endpoint, into a sequence of switch configurations.
2) Training Traffic: Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism
split a training job across the accelerators. Mixture-of-experts
(MoE) models add expert parallelism, which spreads specialist
parts of the model, the experts, across the job’s worker
processes and routes each token to a few of them [5], [22].
Expert dispatch is an all-to-all collective. Its demand matrix
is dense within each expert group and sparse across groups,
and it shifts as some experts draw more tokens than others.
FoldFit schedules these matrices in Section IV.
Published runs show the scale: Llama 3 was trained on about
16,000 GPUs [23], MegaScale scaled training past 10,000 [24],
DeepSeek-V3 used 2,048 [25], and Meta reports training on
the order of 100,000 GPUs [26]. At this scale hardware is the
main threat. Llama 3 attributed about 78% of its unexpected
interruptions to confirmed or suspected hardware issues [23].
A study of two large research clusters reports a mean time
to failure of 7.9 hours for 1,024-GPU jobs; InfiniBand link
failures were among the top causes of job failures, and most
of those came in one short burst from a handful of nodes [27].
Meta’s report on a 32,000-GPU job counts 2.3 interruptions per
1,000 servers per day, 78% of them hardware-related, and Meta
estimates one failure every 18 minutes at 100,000 GPUs [26].
B. Optical Data Plane in a Data Center Network
Fig. 1 shows the four optical layers of the data plane.
a) The CPO data plane: CPO moves the photonic engines
from the rack edge onto the switch or accelerator package, and
the light source changes with them: a shared pool of external
lasers, in field-replaceable modules, replaces one laser per
engine. Each NVIDIA Quantum-X package uses 18 photonic
engines fed by 36 laser inputs [28]. The light comes from
external laser modules of eight lasers each, and one module
powers 32 of the switch’s 576 transmit lanes [9], which implies
18 modules and 144 lasers per switch; the 36 laser inputs above
describe a single package. The OIF implementation agreement
for external laser modules, the external laser small form-factor
pluggable (ELSFP), allows an optional thermoelectric cooler
and replacement at the faceplate [29]. An analyst reports
that each related Spectrum-X package carries 36 photonic
engines, 32 active and four held in reserve for redundancy [28];
NVIDIA’s own description of the single-ASIC version lists 32
engines fed by 16 laser modules and mentions no reserve [9].


--- Page 4 ---
4
We apply that proportion of engines to the laser pool, so
32 active channels backed by a four-laser reserve is this
paper’s calibration point throughout, and every later use of
the four-laser reserve rests on this assumption. Other vendors
also use external lasers. Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6-Davisson,
sampling since October 2025, places 102.4 Tb/s of CPO behind
field-replaceable ELSFP laser modules. Light sources are also
changing form. Lightmatter’s Guide is a one-rack-unit light
engine whose output would otherwise take about 18 ELSFP
modules [30]. Lumentum has announced an eight-wavelength
dense-WDM ELSFP with initial availability in the first half of
2027 [31]. How many lasers share an enclosure, the grouping
behind the module-level correlation of Section V-V-A, therefore
varies by design. The alternative keeps the optics in a pluggable
module that can be serviced on its own. Mesh Optical’s linear-
pluggable optics drop the digital signal processor that retimes
and equalizes the signal, and the vendor reports a draw under
10 watts at 1.6 Tb/s [32]. NVIDIA, which reported Spectrum-X
Photonics in full production in June 2026, presents it as giving
five times the power efficiency and five times the AI uptime
of networks built on pluggable transceivers [33].
b) Optical circuit switching and MoE traffic: Jupiter
brought optical circuit switching to data center scale under
software-defined control [2], [34], and Sirius to nanosecond
switching [35]. An earlier system, Helios, paired electrical
packet switching with optical circuit switching in modular data
centers and reconfigured the circuits as traffic shifted [36]. Other
work ties the topology to the training job. TopoOpt optimizes
the topology together with the parallelization strategy [37],
and MixNet exploits the locality of expert parallelism in
MoE training, beating a topology optimizer by 1.5× and
1.3× in its reported comparisons [5]. For scheduling, circuit
switches classically use a Birkhoff–von Neumann (BvN)
decomposition [38], which meets the busiest-port lower bound
on the makespan, the total time the schedule holds its circuits,
but does so by splitting demands across as many as (P −1)2+1
configurations for P ports, each paying a reconfiguration delay.
Faster heuristics, such as MixNet’s greedy reconfiguration [5],
state no worst-case bound. Research schedulers model the
cost of switching explicitly. Solstice schedules hybrid circuit
and packet switches by heuristic and lands within 14% of
optimal at scale, without a worst-case bound [39]. Eclipse
carries a constant-factor guarantee on the traffic a circuit switch
serves within a fixed time window [40], and Sunflow finishes
a coflow, a group of flows that completes together, within 2×
of the optimal time [41]. Solstice and Eclipse halt the whole
switch for a delay δ at every change of configuration, and
Sunflow halts only the ports being reconfigured. Work from
2025 and 2026 schedules circuit switches for machine-learning
jobs specifically. Chronos derives circuit schedules ahead of
time from the training program, leaving expert parallelism
as the one pattern it must schedule on demand [42]. Spectra
schedules one AI demand matrix across parallel circuit switches
with the reconfiguration delay in the objective [43], LACE and
Flux compile reconfiguration schedules from the structure of
the whole workload [44], [45], DELTA engineers one static
topology from the job’s dependency graph [46], OMLSched
schedules jobs on optical ML clusters [47], and Silverstone
reconfigures the fabric across the phases of disaggregated
RL [48]. Amponsah and Addanki show that the many matchings
of a BvN decomposition fragment MoE execution into small
batches [49]. Coflow schedulers for parallel and multi-core
circuit switches now carry worst-case guarantees with the
reconfiguration delay in the model [50], [51]; Chen’s makespan
ratio grows with the number of flows at a port. Section IV-IV-B
sets out how the decomposition works, what it costs, and how
FoldFit’s bound compares with these.
c) Microring stabilization and module reliability: A
microring modulator responds to light only near one particular
wavelength, its resonance, and that wavelength moves with
temperature. A standard 220-nm silicon ring’s resonance shifts
about 77 pm/°C near 1550 nm [52], and our model uses
70 pm/°C as a representative value. In NVIDIA’s design the
lasers that feed it sit in a temperature-controlled module [9], so
it is the ring’s drift, not the laser’s, that the link must track. Once
a ring drifts past the largest offset the receiver tolerates, the
receiver loses lock on it. Parts in the field stabilize the ring by
reactive dither locking: the controller varies the ring’s setting
slightly and reads how the output responds. That response
shows which way the resonance has moved, so the correction
comes only after an offset has appeared. A ring reacquires
lock in roughly 200 µs [53], and its link carries nothing until
it does. Integrated thermal stabilization of individual microring
modulators has also been demonstrated in hardware [54], model-
predictive and feedforward control of microring modulators
has been designed in simulation [55], and locking driven by
the bit error rate now tracks 71.4 nm/s with no measurable
error-rate penalty under a 40 °C disturbance [56]. Closest to
ThermaLead, Yoon et al. show that the compute bursts of
MoE training heat a wafer-scale optical interconnect by several
kelvin within milliseconds and stall its rings unless the heater
is pre-driven from GPU kernel launches or the tracking loop
runs much faster [57]. ThermaLead instead forecasts the drift
from temperature telemetry.
Lumentum has demonstrated two external laser modules
delivering 16 channels on a 200 GHz grid at about 24 dBm
per channel [58], and Sirius-class tunable lasers switch within
912 ps [35]. However, the open issue for the laser modules is
reliability: how many spare lasers a pool must hold. In [59], it
was showed that an integrated laser, which cannot be cooled
and runs at the 70 °C maximum chip temperature, needs a
backup laser to meet a 1% annual failure-rate target, whereas an
external source can be cooled by a thermoelectric cooler [59].
Pooling needs far fewer spares than a backup per laser: tunable-
laser sparing restores a 32-wavelength link with only 4–8
shared spares under moderate load [21]. Neither analysis
models correlated laser failures, so both correspond to the
zero-correlation case, ρ →0, to which the coverage model
of Section IV-IV-A reduces. Studies of distributed storage
show the cost of that omission. In Google’s storage fleet,
failing to model correlated node failures typically overestimated
availability by at least two orders of magnitude [60], and
random replica placement is almost guaranteed to lose data
when a cluster-wide power outage takes many nodes down at
once [61]. We found no published vendor pool-sizing rule with
a coverage guarantee.


--- Page 5 ---
5
d) Formal tools: Coverage bounds, the MULTIFIT pack-
ing ratios of Section IV-IV-B, one-step-ahead prediction, and
threshold protection are the four formal tools this paper builds
on. All four have a long record in optical WDM survivability
and scheduling [17]–[21]. That work targeted fiber cuts at
gigabit rates. The AI data center adds correlated thermal stress
on shared laser pools and on microrings running at 200 Gb/s
per lane, and each component here is designed anew for that
setting.
III. LASER POOLING: THE CORRELATION CEILING
Pooling spares works like insurance, and it fails for the
same reason. Ten thousand houses in different towns burn
independently, so a small reserve covers the year’s claims. Ten
thousand houses on one floodplain produce every claim in a
single flood, and insuring more houses there adds exposure
without diversifying it. Co-packaged lasers that share cooling
and power resemble the floodplain: one shared cause can bring
a burst of failures that overwhelms spares sized for scattered
ones.
A. Mathematical Model
Definitions: We need to know whether the spares in a
pool cover the lasers that fail in a window. Consider a pool
of N lasers whose failures are exchangeable, meaning that no
laser is special: any set of k lasers is as likely to be the failing
set as any other. Failures are counted over a fixed window of
time: F is the number that fail in one window, and F = F/N
is the failure fraction. The window is the restock interval, the
time a pool runs before its failed modules are replaced and its
spares refilled, and every coverage and availability figure in
this paper is a per-window quantity. One laser’s probability of
failing during one window is its marginal failure probability
λ, which later sections also call its per-window failure rate, so
λ = 0.05 means a one-in-twenty chance per laser per window.
Laser reliability is usually quoted as a FIT rate, failures per
109 device hours, and a laser at φ FIT with a window of tw
hours has λ = 1 −exp(−φ tw × 10−9). The failure correlation
ρ ∈(0, 1), the pairwise (intraclass) correlation between failures,
measures how strongly failures cluster. As ρ →0 the failures
become independent. A larger ρ means that a greater share
of failures traces to one cause acting on many lasers at once.
Against those failures the pool holds s spare lasers, giving a
spare ratio σ = s/N. Deployments cap the ratio, and we write
the budget cap as σmax; the cap assumed throughout is the 2×
pool, in which spares equal active lasers. The severity of the
shared cause varies from window to window, and we model it
with the beta distribution whose mean is λ and whose intraclass
correlation is ρ. Its shape parameters are a = λ(1 −ρ)/ρ and
b = (1 −λ)(1 −ρ)/ρ. Laser availability, which we also call
coverage, is the probability that the spares cover every failure
in a window, written AN(σ). The rest of the paper states it as
a percentage in the industry’s notation, such as 99.999%, and
figures plot it on a logarithmic scale of 1 −AN labelled the
same way. Table I lists the notation used throughout the paper.
Theorem 1 (Correlation ceiling). For the system described
above, all of the following hold:

NOTATION USED THROUGHOUT THE PAPER.
1) F converges almost surely to a random level Θ ∼
Beta(a, b), and Var(F) →λ(1 −λ)ρ > 0.
2) Availability, AN(σ) = Pr[F ≤σN] →A∗(σ; λ, ρ) =
FBeta(σ; a, b).
That is, as a laser pool operating at a fixed value of σ
grows, its availability approaches a limit below one that
does not depend on N.
3) Given a budget cap on the spare ratio, σ ≤σmax < 1,
the availability a pool can approach as it grows is at
most A∗(σmax; λ, ρ) < 1, so for any target above it,
every large enough pool held to that cap falls short of
the target.
4) For every σ > λ, A∗→1 as ρ →0, so the ceiling of a
2× pool reaches any target once ρ is low enough.
Under independent failures the variance of the failure fraction
shrinks as 1/N, so a bigger pool is a safer pool. Part (1) says
that under correlation the same variance flattens onto a floor,
and past a few hundred lasers the extra hardware buys almost
nothing.
Proof. Everything turns on one object, the latent common-
cause level Θ that de Finetti’s theorem [10] guarantees behind
any exchangeable failure process that can be extended to an
arbitrarily large pool. By de Finetti, an infinite exchangeable
binary sequence is a mixture of i.i.d. Bernoulli sequences:
there is a latent Θ with Xi | Θ i.i.d. Bernoulli(Θ), where
Xi indicates the failure of laser i. Read operationally, this
says that if no laser is special and the pool could be extended
indefinitely, it must behave as though a hidden severity level
Θ were drawn first for the window, after which each laser fails
independently at that level. Correlation is then what happens
when Θ varies between windows, and the beta-binomial model
assumes that a single scalar, ρ, is enough to describe how much
it varies. The beta-binomial model is the case Θ ∼Beta(a, b),
with the parameters chosen so that E[Θ] = λ and Var(Θ) =


--- Page 6 ---
6
λ(1 −λ)ρ, which makes the pairwise correlation of the Xi
equal to Var[Θ]/[λ(1−λ)] = ρ. Each part below is a statement
about that latent level.
Part (1). Conditional on Θ, the failure count F = P
i Xi
is Binomial(N, Θ), so the strong law of large numbers gives
F/N →Θ almost surely, and unconditionally the limit is Θ.
The law of total variance then gives
Var(F/N) = E[Θ(1 −Θ)]
N
+ Var[Θ]
= λ(1 −λ)[1 + (N −1)ρ]
N
,
whose limit is λ(1 −λ)ρ (= 0.0071 at the operating point of
Section III-III-B).
Part (2). Coverage at spare ratio σ holds if and only if
F/N ≤σ, so, since F/N →Θ almost surely and FBeta is
continuous, AN(σ) →Pr[Θ ≤σ] = FBeta(σ; a, b). That limit
stays below one for σ < 1, because Beta(a, b) puts positive
mass on (σ, 1].
Part (3). Since AN(σ) is nondecreasing in σ, a pool held
to σ ≤σmax has AN(σ) ≤AN(σmax), which converges to
FBeta(σmax; a, b) < 1 by Part (2); the cap bounds the limit,
not every finite N.
Part (4). As ρ →0, a+b = (1−ρ)/ρ grows without bound
and Var(Θ) = λ(1 −λ)ρ →0, so Θ concentrates at its mean
λ < σ and A∗→1.
Parts (2) and (3) describe the limit, and a finite pool can
sit slightly above it: at the stress point, a large pool at the
four-laser reserve’s spare ratio of 1/9 approaches 85.1%, below
the coverage of the 32-channel reserve itself (Section IV-IV-A).
At the 2× cap and ρ = 0.15, every pool size we evaluated
approaches the ceiling from below, so there the ceiling of a
2× pool is a true upper limit. Part (4) states only the limit.
Concentration alone does not make A∗monotone in ρ at every
σ: for a spare ratio only slightly above λ, a more correlated
pool can hold more of its mass below σ, as the left panel of
Fig. 3 shows below a spare ratio of about 14%. At σ = 1/2 we
verified numerically that ∂A∗/∂ρ < 0 over ρ ∈(0, 1) for every
λ ≤0.3, so at the 2× cap the ceiling A∗strictly increases as
ρ falls.
B. Analysis
The theorem supplies no value for λ or ρ, and every
number below moves with both. The analysis takes a stress
operating point of λ = 0.05 and ρ = 0.15. When the per-
laser failure probability is small, ρ is the common-cause beta
factor of reliability engineering: the share of failures that
trace back to a single shared cause. Other industries have
estimated it. IEC 61508-6 assigns values from 0.005 to 0.05
for programmable electronics and from 0.01 to 0.10 for field
equipment, according to the defenses in place [12], and nuclear
practice uses 0.05 to 0.10 for a redundant pair [11], [62].
Where the units share one die, IEC 61508-2 starts from 0.33
and accepts the redundancy as adequately separated only once
the estimate is shown to be below 0.25 [63].
Lasers in one module have little physical separation, since
they share its enclosure and temperature control and often
101

variance of failure fraction
Fig. 2. Why correlated failures do not average out: the variance of the failure
fraction F against pool size N, on logarithmic axes. With independent failures
(falling line) the variance shrinks as 1/N. With correlation (ρ = 0.15, upper
curve) it flattens at the floor λ(1 −λ)ρ = 0.0071 [derived].
one power supply, so a pool built from a few such modules
sits away from the well-separated end of that range. We
therefore take ρ = 0.15, between the 0.10 upper end of the
IEC 61508-6 and nuclear ranges and the 0.25 on-die limit, as an
estimate for a well-engineered package, a pool-wide value that
Section V-V-A splits into within-module and across-module
parts. It is an assumption, not a measurement: no field data for
these laser form factors pins it down yet, and Section VII-VII-E
describes the experiment that would. The choice is pessimistic
for availability and favorable to our argument, since a lower ρ
would raise the ceiling of Theorem 1 and so weaken the case
for decorrelating. We also report the full ρ-sweep, including a
plausible band of ρ ∈[0.08, 0.35] for the cost results.
The failure probability needs the same care, because the
window turns a FIT rate into a probability. The OIF co-
packaging framework sets a reliability target of 50 FIT for the
laser source of each 3.2 Tb/s engine over a six-year service
life [64]. The target covers a whole source, and a source can
hold several lasers, as NVIDIA’s eight-laser module does, so
applying 50 FIT to each laser is a pessimistic reading of it. An
average optical transceiver runs at about 200 to 300 FIT, and
low-cost lasers recently deployed in data centers failed at ten
times their target rate [65]. Against those figures, λ = 0.05 is a
stress setting: it is what a laser at about 1,000 FIT accumulates
when it is never replaced over a six-year life. For co-packaged
optics, Broadcom reports one million 400G-equivalent port-
hours without a link flap in Meta’s high-temperature lab [66],
which caps the per-port flap rate near 3,000 FIT at 95%
confidence, above both 50 FIT and the stress setting. Table II
evaluates the same pool at rates nearer the targets. For the
32-channel pool at ρ = 0.15, 99.999% stops fitting inside the
2× cap once λ exceeds about 2.4 × 10−4 per window. That
happens when the FIT rate times the restock interval passes
about 2.4 × 105 FIT-hours, after about 200 days at 50 FIT and
about 40 days at 250 FIT.
Fig. 2 shows Part (1) at this operating point: the failure
fraction keeps a standard deviation of 0.084 however large the
pool grows.

TURNS A LASER FIT RATE φ AND A RESTOCK INTERVAL tw INTO THE
PER-WINDOW PROBABILITY λ. Acrit IS THE LARGE-POOL CEILING OF A 2×
POOL (COROLLARY 1), AND THE 32-CHANNEL POOL REACHES SLIGHTLY
LESS. s5 IS THAT POOL’S SPARE COUNT FOR 99.999% COVERAGE,
CORRELATED AND INDEPENDENT; THE 2× CAP ALLOWS 32, WHICH SETS

operating point requires a spare ratio of σ = 0.821. Since
σ = s/N, the total pool must then be 1/(1 −σ) ≈5.6× the
active laser count, which no deployment would carry; that is
the large-pool limit, and Section IV-IV-A gives the finite-pool
answer in whole lasers.
Corollary 1 (Critical availability). Given a budget cap σmax,
the value Acrit = FBeta(σmax; a, b) acts as a threshold for
large pools: a target below Acrit is reachable with a spare
ratio inside the cap once the pool is large enough, while a
target at or above it cannot be reached by any ratio inside the
cap, and the pool multiple 1/(1 −σ) it would demand grows
without bound as the target approaches one. For a 2× pool
at the stress rate, Acrit = 99.670% at ρ = 0.15, rising above
99.999% once ρ falls below about 0.056.
At this operating point no spare ratio inside the cap reaches
99.999%, and a low enough correlation does, since the ceiling
of a 2× pool tends to one as ρ falls (Part (4) of Theorem 1).
Section V-V-B prices decorrelation, and the right panel of
Fig. 3 shows the rise for a fixed 2× pool.
Fast recovery offers a partial second route toward 99.999%,
because it shortens an exhaustion that coverage fails to prevent.
Coverage ignores how long an exhaustion lasts, and effective
availability also counts how quickly it is repaired. Take a
pool sized for 99.9% coverage, which is 49 spares on the
32-channel calibration point of Section IV-IV-A. TriageGuard
(Section IV-IV-D) keeps hot spares pre-wired to the modules
most likely to fail, so a failure on such a module switches
to its hot spare in milliseconds instead of lasting the rest of
the window, and those hot spares sit outside the shared pool,
so they are still there when the pool runs out. Only failures
on the pre-spared modules are shortened, however. Under the
exchangeable failures of Theorem 1 every module carries the
same risk, so hot spares on 4 of the 18 modules see on average
4/18, about 22%, of the failures in an exhausted window,
and a risk ranking raises that share only as far as module
risks differ and are predicted (Section IV-IV-D). Fast recovery
therefore narrows the gap to 99.999% by an amount we have
not computed, and replacements must also keep arriving to
restock the pool.
The pairing of coverage and fast recovery has two further
limits. First, those 49 spares make a 2.5× pool before the
hot spares are counted. That is less than a third of the 156
spares the coverage-only route needs, but the pairing is not
shown to reach 99.999%, and even its starting pool sits above
the 2× budget cap, so fast recovery cannot bring the target
inside the cap. Only decorrelation, priced in Section V-V-B,
fits inside the cap. Second, LightReserve counts spares in
lasers while TriageGuard hands out hot spares a module at a
time, so combining them in a deployment requires fixing the
modules-of-lasers shape of Section V-V-A first.
IV. PROPOSED CONTROL PLANE DESIGN
This section presents the details of the proposed Halley
framework. Four components, one per layer, sit above the
optical data plane, as shown in Fig. 4. Table III lists the
decision each one makes, its guarantee or, for ThermaLead, its
benchmark, and its reactive fallback. All four follow one rule:
each acts on a prediction of its layer’s next state, and when its
forecast is stale or unsure, it steps aside and the system runs

A. LightReserve: Sizing the Laser Pool
LightReserve decides how many spares a shared laser pool
carries. Operators fix the number once, as a static n+k
reserve, and hold it whatever the failure rate turns out to
be. LightReserve computes it from the failure rate and from
how strongly the failures are correlated, and returns it with a
provable coverage guarantee for those inputs.
Algorithm 1 models the total pool N = n + s and not the
active set alone, because the spares are themselves failure-prone.

UNREACHABLE and, in place of a spare count, emits the
correlation ρ′ that would bring the target under the ceiling,
which turns an impossible sparing problem into a concrete
decorrelation target.

1: input: demand matrix D, channel capacity C, channel

for 99% coverage at λ = 0.05, 9 at 0.10, and 16 at 0.20. As
ρ →0 the method reduces to that known result.
At λ = 0.05 and ρ = 0.15 the four-laser reserve gives
A(4) = 86.3%, and 99% coverage needs 23 spare lasers
where independence needed 5. Reaching 99.9% takes 49, and
99.999% takes 156, a 5.9× pool. The algorithm flags that
pool as UNREACHABLE and returns a correlation target in
its place: 99.999% within a 2× pool of 32 channels needs
ρ ≤0.046, a little below the large-pool value of about
0.056 in Corollary 1. The flag concerns coverage only; fast
recovery (Section III-III-B) narrows the effective-availability
gap, without a computed guarantee and from a pool still above
the cap.
The right panel sweeps the failure rate: the fixed reserve’s
coverage falls steeply as the rate grows, while a pool that
LightReserve sizes to each rate holds its 99.9% target, though
above about λ = 0.02 that sizing needs more than the 32 spares
the 2× cap allows. For 99.999% coverage, which the panel
does not plot, the correlation limits the pool more than the rate
does: at ρ = 0.15, even λ = 0.005, a tenth of the stress rate,
still needs 76 spares, more than twice the 32 the cap allows.
Only a rate below about 2.4 × 10−4 brings 99.999% inside the
cap (Table II), whereas lowering ρ cuts the count at every rate.
B. FoldFit: Scheduling the Circuit Switch
FoldFit schedules the OCS that joins the photonic engines to
one another. The switch holds only a limited set of connections
at a time, so a communication phase is served as a sequence
of configurations, each held for a while before the switch is
reconfigured. A good sequence is short, because the collective
waits while each configuration is held, and stable, because
every reconfiguration costs switching time. FoldFit chooses
the sequence by recasting the problem as packing: each traffic
demand becomes a job, and the jobs are packed onto the
parallel circuits the switch can hold at once.
The fabric is a single-stage OCS with crossbar semantics. At
any moment it holds one configuration, a set of port-disjoint
circuits, meaning that no two of them share a switch port.
Traffic between two engines flows only while a circuit connects
them, so serving a workload means choosing a sequence of
configurations and a dwell time for each. Those dwells sum to
the makespan of Section II-II-B. Each change of configuration
also costs a fixed switching delay δ, which the makespan as
defined here leaves out. The input is the demand matrix D,
with entry Dij the traffic engine i must send to engine j,
expressed in time slots at the per-channel capacity C.
The classical way to choose that sequence is the BvN
decomposition [38], which pads the demand matrix until every
row and column sums to the busiest port’s load and writes it as
a weighted sum of permutation matrices, each a configuration
whose weight is its dwell. The dwells then meet the busiest-port
bound, but over as many as (P −1)2 + 1 configurations for
P ports, most with tiny dwells, each costing a reconfiguration
delay that nothing in the decomposition bounds.
FoldFit replaces the decomposition with a packing, a problem
that has carried a worst-case makespan bound since the 1970s.
FoldFit treats each nonzero demand as an indivisible job
of length Dij slots and the fabric as m identical service
channels, where m is the number of port-disjoint circuits
one configuration can sustain. These channels are the parallel
machines of the packing problem, not the wavelength channels
of the laser pool. The target is OPT, the shortest schedule
that serves all jobs on m parallel channels without two circuits


--- Page 10 ---
10
sharing a port at the same time. Dropping the port condition
leaves the classical makespan problem, whose optimum is no
longer.
Three lower bounds on that optimum are immediate. No
schedule beats the largest single demand; none beats the average
load P
ij Dij/m; and none beats the busiest port’s total traffic,
the largest row or column sum of D, because a port carries
one circuit at a time. Starting from those bounds, Algorithm 2
binary-searches the deadline T, a candidate makespan, running
FFD at each candidate T. FFD sorts the jobs from longest to
shortest and places each in turn on the first channel whose
load would stay within T. If every job fits, T is feasible. The
deadline T ∗on which the search ends fixes the assignment of
jobs to channels.
Binary-searched FFD is the MULTIFIT algorithm of multi-
processor scheduling, here with its search started at Tlb, and
it inherits the MULTIFIT theorem. On identical channels,
q steps of the search give T ∗≤(1.22 + 2−q) OPT [67],
and Yue tightened the constant to the exact ratio, T ∗≤
(13/11 + 2−q) OPT [68]. Both bounds are stated against
the classical optimum, which is no longer than OPT. Every
deadline at which FFD fails lies below 13/11 of the classical
optimum, the search starts at Tlb ≤OPT, and its upper end,
max{Tlb, P D/m + max D}, keeps the search interval no
wider than the classical optimum, so both ratios hold against
OPT. They need not hold against the classical optimum itself,
which the busiest-port bound can exceed several times over.
With five or more steps Yue’s guarantee sits below 11/9, the
figure we quote throughout. Under the three conditions below,
the schedule is then never more than 22% longer than the
optimum however the demand matrix moves, and the exact
bound narrows that margin toward 18% as q grows.
MULTIFIT is a result about m identical machines, and it
applies to a switch under three conditions. First, the channels
have to be interchangeable, which holds while every circuit
runs at the same per-channel capacity C. Second, each demand
has to be packed as one indivisible job on one channel. Third,
FFD’s assignment of jobs to channels has to be realizable as a
sequence of port-disjoint configurations.
The classical setting does not supply the third condition,
because two jobs sitting on different channels may share a
switch port, and no configuration can run both at once. We call
the step that turns the assignment into port-disjoint configura-
tions the alignment. The busiest-port bound is necessary for an
alignment to exist at all, which is why the binary search starts
no lower than it. When a demand may be split at a configuration
boundary, which is the relaxation BvN works in, the alignment
is exact and the 11/9 guarantee carries over untouched. When
demands are strictly unsplittable, the alignment can leave idle
gaps that the 11/9 bound does not account for, and the worked
example below loses one slot this way. On the workloads swept
in Section V-V-F, FoldFit’s makespan lands within 6% of the
larger of the first two lower bounds above on every instance,
and within about 1% on average from 16 engines up. The
simulation packs jobs onto channels without the port condition,
so that evidence covers the packing and says nothing about
alignment gaps; Section VII-VII-D records the unsplittable
case as open.
One refinement adapts the packing to MoE traffic. Expert-
parallel demand is block-structured and drifts slowly as expert
popularity shifts. When several placements tie during FFD,
FoldFit keeps jobs from the same expert-parallel block in the
same configuration, so consecutive scheduling rounds reproduce
the same configurations and the switch can hold them instead of
rebuilding them. The simulation of Section V-V-F replaces first
fit with this preference and, failing it, the least-loaded channel,
so it evaluates a variant that the 11/9 proof does not cover.
Its baseline, a longest-processing-time (LPT) list schedule that
places one demand in five on a random channel, spreads every
block over every channel. Against it, FoldFit cuts a proxy for
reconfigurations, the number of distinct expert blocks each
channel serves, by 45% at 16 engines. At 8 engines, a single
block, the two tie.
Fig. 6 works through a 4 × 4 MoE demand matrix, dense
on the expert-block diagonal with entries of 9, 8, 7, and 6
slots and light off the diagonal. The busiest port carries 11
slots, so no schedule is shorter than 11, and Algorithm 2’s
search stops at that bound, T ∗= 11. Turning the packing into
port-disjoint configurations costs one more slot: C1 carries the
diagonal entries and dwells 9 slots, C2 the exchanges inside
each two-engine expert block for 2, and C3 the cross-block
residual for 1. The makespan is 12 slots before switching delay,
a ratio of 1.09 to the lower bound; the extra slot is an alignment
loss that the 11/9 ≈1.22 guarantee does not cover, and the
ratio still falls inside it. A BvN decomposition of the same
matrix meets the 11-slot bound on dwell by splitting demands;
the decomposition we computed uses five configurations to
FoldFit’s three, so it pays the switching delay δ five times
instead of three.
a) How this differs from MixNet: MixNet [5] exploits
the same expert-parallel locality and reconfigures the switch
in advance from a prediction of the first all-to-all’s demand,
but gives no worst-case bound, so on an adversarial shift
its makespan is unconstrained. FoldFit adds a bound that
holds however MoE traffic moves mid-training, under the three
conditions above.
b) How this compares with circuit-switch schedulers:
Sunflow [41] finishes a single coflow within 2× of the optimal
time for any reconfiguration delay δ, and its bound already
counts the delay of every reconfiguration it makes. FoldFit’s
11/9 is tighter but narrower. It bounds the dwell time T ∗,
and a schedule with kr reconfigurations takes T ∗+ krδ in
all, a second term the bound does not cover. Commercial
OCSs typically switch in 10–20 ms [69], so with the worked
example’s three configurations that term stays under 1% of
the dwell only for phases of 3–6 s or longer, and rescheduling
within one MoE layer’s dispatch would need microsecond-class
or faster switching [35]. Keeping the shorter of the FoldFit
and Sunflow schedules bounds the total by the smaller of
(11/9) OPT + krδ and twice Sunflow’s optimum, in Sunflow’s
switch model. Solstice [39] minimizes a similar total, dwell
time plus δ per configuration, by heuristic and without a worst-
case guarantee. Eclipse [40] maximizes the traffic served within
a fixed window, a different objective.
c) Why the tighter bound matters: Plain LPT list schedul-
ing carries Graham’s 4/3−1/(3m) ratio [70]. That ratio equals

11/9 at m = 3 and is tighter at m = 2, so the quoted 11/9

shows the canonical worst case for list scheduling: six unit
demands followed by one three-slot demand on m = 3 channels.
A greedy scheduler serving demands in arrival order spreads
the six unit jobs across all three channels and must then run the
long job alone, for a makespan of 5 slots against an optimum
of 3. That is 5/3 ≈1.67× optimal, exactly Graham’s 2−1/m
bound for list scheduling at m = 3 [70]. FFD’s decreasing
order places the long job first and stays exactly optimal here.
Expert popularity shifting mid-training or mid-serving can
produce orderings of exactly this shape.
C. ThermaLead: Steadying the Microring
The receiver loses lock once the ring’s resonance offset
exceeds the lock threshold, the largest offset it tolerates. Parts in
the field use the reactive dither locking of Section II-II-B, which
corrects an offset only after observing it, so the receiver absorbs
each step’s drift before the correction lands. ThermaLead adds
a feedforward term. It predicts the next-step drift from a short
history and pre-positions the heater one step early, so the
receiver sees only the error of that forecast. The heater and its
authority are the same in both schemes; only the excursion,
the swing of the offset at the receiver, changes.
In Algorithm 3, x[t] is the ring’s resonance offset at control
step t, in picometers via the 70 pm/°C slope. The 8-sample
moving average of line 2 costs an adder and a shift, so it is
cheap enough to sit beside the local servo, the circuit that sets
the heater from the temperature error, which Section VI builds
in hardware. The residual r[t+1] of line 4 is the part of the
drift that the predictor missed and that is left for the receiver.
ThermaLead’s benchmark is the residual of the best one-step
predictor from the previous sample. We model the drift x[t]
as wide-sense stationary over the window the predictor sees.
Its variance is σ2
x (this subsection’s σ is a standard deviation
of the resonance offset, not the spare ratio of Section III),
and its lag-1 autocorrelation R is the correlation between one
step’s offset and the next. By the orthogonality principle of
estimation theory, the minimum-mean-square-error predictor
leaves residual variance σ2
e = σ2
x(1 −R2) < σ2
x, the best
any predictor can do from the previous sample alone. The
expression is exact for AR(1) drift; the evaluation’s trace adds
a periodic heat cycle to an AR(1) process with noise bursts,
so on that trace it is an approximation. The moving average of
line 2 is a cheaper forecast that extrapolates the recent slope.
It uses eight samples, so the bound above does not cover it,
and the simulation below measures what it achieves.
Treat the offset as Gaussian, a modeling assumption that the
trace below satisfies only approximately. An offset of standard
deviation σ then exceeds the lock threshold τ with probability
2¯Φ(τ/σ) on any given step, where ¯Φ is the standard normal
upper-tail probability. Shrinking σ from σx to σe therefore
strictly lowers the lock-loss rate, and the larger R is, the larger
the gain.
The lock-loss argument fixes neither the threshold nor the
control step. The lock-loss rate depends on the threshold only
through the ratio τ/σ, so shrinking σ lowers the rate wherever
a particular receiver’s threshold sits. The control step is only a
unit of counting: the analysis and the counts below are both
per step, and any reduction is a ratio of two per-step counts,
so no particular duration is assumed. The step must be short
against the thermal time constant, so that a one-step-ahead
forecast has something to predict, and long enough for the
heater to act. Section VI shows that the heater drive is not the
binding constraint; the heater’s own thermal response is.
The evaluation models the thermal environment of training
as a periodic heat cycle, a sinusoid with an 8 °C swing and
a period of 120 control steps. The cycle stands for the bulk-
synchronous alternation in which each compute phase heats
the die and each communication phase lets it cool. On top of
it sits an AR(1) residual with coefficient 0.8, whose noise has
a standard deviation of 0.55 °C on a random 30% of steps and
0.12 °C on the rest. The lock threshold is 25 pm. We treat this
trace as a stress case.
In simulation the deployed dither lock cancels every offset
once it has observed it, so the receiver sees each step’s full drift.
On the stress trace the dither lock loses lock on 462 of every
2000 control steps and ThermaLead on 472, averaged over 30
seeds. Paired seed by seed, ThermaLead loses lock 2% more
often (p = 0.003, paired t-test) and does worse on 22 of the 30
seeds. Its residual variance is 1.3% above the drift’s own, so its
forecast removes nothing. The closed form above explains part
of this. The drift’s lag-1 autocorrelation is only 0.075, so even
the best linear forecast from the previous sample could remove
less than 1% of its variance. The trace is not unforecastable,
however. An oracle forecast that knows the trace’s sinusoid and
noise state, a bound and not a controller, would cut the count
to 315, 32% below the dither lock. ThermaLead gains as the
drift gets smoother. When noise bursts hit 10% of steps instead
of 30%, it loses lock 22% less often than the dither lock, and
with no bursts 78% less often. A gate on the forecast’s own
error removes the stress-trace deficit. Applied only while its
mean absolute error over the last 16 steps is below the raw
drift’s, the gated controller loses lock on 452 steps, 2.1% fewer
than the dither lock and better on 23 of the 30 seeds, and
keeps at least 95% of the forecast’s gain on smoother traces.
The rule was fixed before any run; other windows and error
measures give 448 to 487, so the result depends on it. On the
burst sweep the drift’s lag-1 autocorrelation was 0.13 or more
wherever ThermaLead helped and 0.075 where it lost, so ring
telemetry could tell an operator which case holds.
ThermaLead is therefore the least proven of the four:
its value depends on how smooth the field’s drift is, and

Algorithm 4 TriageGuard risk-ranked selective protection
1: input: risk scores r1 ≥· · · ≥rM, budget B, threshold τ,
switch tsw (5 ms), miss tmiss (150 ms)
2: pre-spare the top-B modules with r > τ
▷fast path
3: route the remainder to the LightReserve pool ▷dynamic

4: on a failure, recovery = tsw if pre-spared, else tmiss
Section VII-VII-D shows its ungated deficit growing under
abrupt transients. ThermaLead also serves as a sensor. The
per-ring temperature telemetry it samples every control step is
the newest thermal signal in the package, and TriageGuard’s
risk ranking runs on it.
D. TriageGuard: Protecting the Modules
A fixed budget of hot spares cannot protect every module,
so the budget should go to the modules most likely to fail.
Deployed systems hand out spares uniformly from the shared
pool. TriageGuard scores each module on its temperature, its
age, and its observed forward-error-correction (FEC) bin, the
band of corrected-error counts the link reports. The result is
the module’s risk score, the estimate of how likely it is to fail.
It then pre-spares every module above a risk threshold τ, up
to the pre-spare budget B, the number of modules that can
hold a hot spare, and routes the rest to the shared pool.
Protecting the top-B risks is optimal, by an exchange
argument. The expected number of protected failures is additive
over the protected set, a sum of one term per protected module.
Swapping a protected low-risk module for an unprotected
higher-risk one never lowers the sum, and repeating such
swaps turns any selection into the top-B selection. Greedy
top-B selection is therefore exactly optimal for any fixed risk
estimate. The argument settles how to spend the budget once
the modules are ranked and says nothing about whether the
ranking is right, so optimality is conditional on the risk estimate,
and the freshness of that estimate dominates the result below.
Algorithm 4 links ranking quality to recovery time. A failure
on a pre-spared module switches to its hot spare in tsw = 5 ms,
while a failure anywhere else draws from the shared pool at
tmiss = 150 ms. Call the share of expected failure probability
that lands on protected modules the intercepted mass µ. The
mean time to recover (MTTR) is µ tsw + (1 −µ) tmiss, so
MTTR falls linearly as the ranking intercepts more of the mass.
Uniform sparing of B modules out of M intercepts B/M of it
on average, and a risk ranking improves on that only as far as
it aims at the modules that will fail. The all-dynamic baseline,
in which every failure draws from the shared pool, bounds the
MTTR of any ranking from above, because a protected failure
can only shorten a repair.
Fig. 7 runs this procedure on the shape of Section II-II-B, 18
field-replaceable modules of 8 lasers each, with hot spares for
4 of the 18; its left panel is a worked example at τ = 0.35. The
simulation draws each module’s true risk from its temperature,
age, and FEC bin, fails each module with a probability that
rises with that risk, and pre-spares the four modules ranked
highest. The ranking sees the true risk through Gaussian error
with a standard deviation of 0.30 on stale telemetry and 0.05
on telemetry that ThermaLead refreshes each step. An oracle
ranks on the true risk itself. Over 30 seeds of 400 episodes,
with every policy scored on the same draws, the stale ranking
intercepts 0.264 of the failures, the fresh ranking 0.307, and
the oracle 0.311. Uniform sparing intercepts 0.222, close to its
expected 4/18. Averaged over the seeds, mean time to recover
falls by 5.1%, 10.4%, and 10.9% against uniform sparing, each
within about one point at 95% confidence. Fresh telemetry thus
recovers nearly all of the oracle’s margin, and that margin is
modest at a budget of 4 modules in 18. The two error levels
are assumptions, not measurements. Field rankings suggest
such concentration is attainable: on a production GPU fleet, a
learned risk ranking catches 64% of future failures in its top
5% of nodes [71], and telemetry-based failure prediction for
optical transceivers reaches an F1 score of 0.89 on production
data [7], [8]. Neither measures the intercepted mass of a co-
packaged module pool. Under these assumptions the fresh
telemetry ThermaLead supplies doubles the cut a stale ranking
achieves, and a field measurement of the intercepted mass is
what would confirm it.

V. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
This section turns the ceiling of Section III into design
guidance and then evaluates the integrated control plane.
Theorem 2 says where in the pool to decorrelate, Observation 1
prices separation against spare lasers, and Observation 2 shows
that the prescription holds across the plausible band of the
correlation. Theorems and propositions are proved, apart from
the steps their proofs mark as numerical checks; an observation
is a computed finding under the cost model stated below.
Section V-V-D reports the integrated goodput, its ablation, and
its tail, and Proposition 1 gives a closed form for the part of that
tail the correlation drives. The relevant software implementation
of these components and the hardware realization is available
at [13].
A. Hierarchical Correlation Ceiling
Lowering the correlation raises the ceiling, but a single
pool-wide correlation gives a designer nothing to act on,
because it does not say which lasers to pull apart from which.
Section III gave every pair of lasers the same correlation ρ.
Deployments are not built that way. The lasers sit in field-
replaceable modules, and a laser shares more with the lasers
in its own module than with the rest of the pool. We model
a shape of 18 modules of 8 lasers, the module count and
module size that NVIDIA’s figures imply for one Quantum-
X switch (Section II-II-B). The active channels and spares
of Section IV-IV-A are drawn from a population of this
kind. A module is the unit of thermal and power isolation,
and separate modules are kept apart by design. Two lasers
in the same module therefore fail together with correlation
ρwithin, and two lasers in different modules with the smaller
ρacross < ρwithin. Reliability engineering treats common causes
in the same grouped way. The alpha-factor and multiple-Greek-
letter models of nuclear safety analysis apply a common
cause within a common-cause component group and treat
separate groups as independent [11], which is the limiting
case ρacross = 0 of the model here.
Consider a pool of M modules holding L lasers each, in
which a single laser fails with marginal probability λ, pairs in
the same module are correlated at ρwithin, and pairs in different
modules at ρacross, with ρwithin ≥ρacross > 0. Concretely, a
pool-wide level Θ0 ∼Beta(a, b) is drawn with a and b set
by λ and ρacross; each module j then draws its own level Θj,
independently given Θ0, from a beta law with mean Θ0 and
intraclass correlation (ρwithin −ρacross)/(1 −ρacross); and the
lasers of module j fail independently at level Θj.
Theorem 2 (Hierarchical ceiling). For the hierarchical system
described above, the following statements hold true:
1) As the module size L grows with M fixed, the failure
fraction F/N has limiting variance λ(1 −λ)[ρacross +
(ρwithin −ρacross)/M], so the within-module term is
suppressed by 1/M, and as modules are added the across-
module correlation sets the floor.
2) As the module size L grows with M fixed, the failure
fraction converges to the average ¯Θ =
1
M
PM
j=1 Θj of
the per-module failure levels, so availability converges
to a ceiling Pr[¯Θ ≤σ] < 1, exactly as in Theorem 1.
3) The flat model of Section III is the exact special case
ρwithin = ρacross.
By Part (1), adding modules averages away the correlation
inside a module and leaves the correlation between modules
untouched, so a designer gains more from separating modules
than from separating the lasers within one.
Proof sketch. Part (1) is the law of total variance applied to the
two exchangeable levels, and the factor 1/M appears because
the within-module component is averaged over M module
draws that are independent given Θ0. Part (2) repeats the law-
of-large-numbers argument of Theorem 1 one module at a time:
condition on the per-module levels Θ1, . . . , ΘM (indexed by
j), and the pool’s failure fraction converges to their average.
Part (3) is immediate, since equal correlations collapse the two
levels into a single beta-binomial, which reproduces the flat
model of Section III digit for digit.
The pool-average pairwise correlation is
¯ρ = nsame ρwithin + ncross ρacross
nsame + ncross
,
where nsame counts the pairs inside one module and ncross the
pairs spanning two. There are ncross =
␀M
2

L2 cross-module
pairs against nsame = M
␀L
2

same-module pairs, a ratio of
(M −1)L/(L−1) that is close to the module count M. At the
18×8 shape that is 9,792 cross-module pairs against 504 same-
module ones, roughly 19 to 1, so ¯ρ tracks the across-module
correlation almost entirely. Evaluated at ¯ρ, the flat, single-level
beta-binomial model of Section III matches the tail of the true
nested process to within about one percentage point from 8
spares up, and to within 0.63 points from 12 spares up. This
shortcut, the flat model evaluated at ¯ρ, is an approximation, so
wherever we use it we also report the nested value.
One objection to co-packaging is that it increases correlation,
and it does, but only within a module. By Theorem 2 the ceiling
rises with separation across modules, and the field-replaceable
faceplate modules of the architecture provide that separation.

Set ρwithin = 0.30 and ρacross = 0.05, and the pool-average
correlation of the 18 × 8 shape becomes ¯ρ = 0.062. Applied
to the 32-channel pool at the 2× budget cap, with the spare
count unchanged, the shortcut lifts coverage from the 99.623%
of the flat model at ρ = 0.15 to 99.993% (Fig. 8), well past
the 99.670% that even a large flat pool approaches. The nested
model confirms the gain: intrepreted as 8 modules of 8, the
32-channel pool has its own ¯ρ = 0.078, at which the shortcut
gives 99.975% and the nested tail 99.985%, so the shortcut
errs low. The full 18 × 8 shape at its own 2× cap reaches
99.997%.
B. Spares Versus Separation
How far to take separation depends on prices, and once
prices are attached the choice between decorrelating and over-
provisioning becomes an optimization with a definite answer.
We state the prices as assumptions: $1,500 per spare laser,
since we found no public price for pluggable laser sources,
and a one-time separation premium of 20% of the active-laser
capital to move a pool from poor separation to good separation.
Neither is a quote. The premium stands in for second sourcing
and for independent power and cooling, which IEC 61508-6
rewards with a lower beta factor [12] but does not price. Every
dollar figure below scales with the per-laser price, so the ratio
between the two paths does not depend on it.
Observation 1 (Optimal split). Under the stated cost model,
given a budget spendable on either spares (raising the spare
ratio) or separation (lowering ρ at the stated premium), the
minimum-cost path to a 99.999% coverage target at the stress
operating point decorrelates the pool first and buys spares
second.
Fig. 9 prices two paths to the same target. A candidate plan
is a pair: a spare count s, and a decorrelation target ρ′ at or
below the pool’s starting correlation ρ0. Its cost is s times the
per-laser price plus the separation premium for reaching ρ′.
Its availability comes from the same beta-binomial coverage

Fig. 10. ρ-invariance. The curves plot the total cost of reaching the coverage
target against how far the pool is decorrelated, one curve for each starting
correlation ρ0. Every curve falls all the way to ρ = 0.03, the best separation
the premium is priced for, so the cheapest plan decorrelates as far as the model

model that Algorithm 1 uses, and the reported point is the
cheapest plan that meets the 99.999% target. Both paths are
priced on coverage alone (spares absorbing every failure), with
no credit for the fast recovery of Section IV-IV-D. Reaching
99.999% coverage by spares alone at ρ = 0.15 takes 156 spare
lasers, about $234,000. Decorrelating to ρ = 0.03 instead costs
about $9,600 in separation premium, which is the 20% figure
applied to the $48,000 of active-laser capital in the 32-channel
pool. That leaves only 23 spare lasers to buy, at $34,500, for
$44,100 in total. Under the stated cost model, separating first
and sizing second therefore reaches the same target at a 5.3×
saving over spares alone. At this premium the ordering is not
close: it would reverse only if separation cost several times the
pool’s entire laser capital. The split depends on the separation-
premium assumption, and a reader with a different premium
can re-solve it with the same coverage model and prices.
C. Optimality with Varying ρ
The plan priced above starts from an assumed correlation,
and ρ has not been measured, so the analysis is weakest here.
We do not defend a particular value of ρ.
Observation 2 (ρ-invariance). Under the stated cost model,
for every starting correlation in the plausible band ρ0 ∈
[0.08, 0.35] the minimum-cost path to the 99.999% coverage
target decorrelates the pool first, toward ρ ≈0.03. The optimal
action never reverses direction within the band.
Fig. 10 sweeps the starting correlation across the band, with
a partial move priced in proportion to the correlation it removes:
$800 for each 0.01, so the move from 0.15 to 0.03 costs the
$9,600 above. A measured value of ρ will therefore set the
size of the saving, not the choice of action.
D. Performance of the Integrated System
Each component has been evaluated alone against the
baseline it replaces, and here their results are composed into
the effective cluster goodput of Section I.


--- Page 15 ---
15
At the stress setting of Section III-III-B, composing the
simulated component results lifts effective cluster goodput from
65.2% to 76.5%, a rise of 11.3 points, or 17.3% in relative
terms (Fig. 11). The full-stack figure is composed by arithmetic
on the component results and is not a separate emulation: the
65.2% baseline, a calibration anchor rather than a simulated
value, is propagated through the simulated availability, lock-
loss, and reconfiguration changes under
goodput = ideal×availability×(1−thermal)×(1−reconfig).
Here
availability
is
the
laser-pool
availability
of
Sec-
tion IV-IV-A, thermal is the share of goodput lost to lock-loss
stalls, and reconfig is the share lost to switch reconfigurations.
The laser pool enters through its per-window coverage, which
depends on the window only through λ.
That availability factor carries an assumption that sets most
of the result. The coverage reading counts a window whose
failures exhaust the spares as lost from start to finish. If only
the dark channels’ bandwidth is lost instead, the availability
factor becomes the expected lit share of the 32 channels; we
call this the lit-share reading. That share is 98.0% for the
four-laser reserve, against its 86.3% coverage, and 99.98% for
the full stack. With the 65.2% anchor held fixed, that reading
lifts the full stack only to 67.4%, a rise of 2.2 points, or 3.4%
relative. Each reading implies its own ideal goodput. A real
job need not fall between the two. When in the window the
spares run out and for how long also move the figure, and this
work models neither. Within the window model, how a job
handles a dark channel is one parameter: if, once the spares
run out, it cannot use a share c of its remaining bandwidth,
the availability factor is c times the coverage plus 1 −c times
the lit share, and the gain rises from 2.2 points at c = 0, a
fabric that routes around a dark channel, to 11.3 at c = 1, a
synchronous job halted until the restock. Every figure below
uses c = 1, the coverage reading.
Each component reports its result in its own units, events
or milliseconds, and the baseline’s two loss shares, thermal
and reconfig, convert the results into goodput. The full stack
keeps each share in proportion to its simulated count, 472/462
for lock-loss events against the dither lock and 8.8/16 for the
proxy count of reconfigurations, and recovery time has no term
in the composition. We have no measured costs, so we set both
baseline shares at three percent, and Section VII-VII-E names
them among the cheaper things to ground on real hardware.
Sweeping the two shares by a factor of two in each direction
moves the baseline across 61.2–67.2% and the full stack across
72.8–78.3%, while the full stack’s gain relative to the baseline
stays within 16.5–18.9%. The relative gain is therefore robust
to the two loss shares, though not to the reading of a shortfall,
and the absolute pair should be read with its band. The released
composite model computes coverage and lit share from the
model of Section III and produces every number in this section.
Fig. 12 isolates each component’s contribution to the key
performance indicators (KPIs). LightReserve contributes the
most, because availability dominates goodput once failures
correlate. Composing the availability gain alone, from 86.3%
to 99.9%, moves goodput from 65.2% to 75.5%. Credited first,
availability therefore accounts for about 10.3 of the 11.3 points,

Fig. 11. The full control plane against the deployed baseline: one bar per
system-level KPI at the stress operating point, each showing the change from
the baseline. Under the coverage reading, goodput rises 11.3 points and pool
availability 13.6 points with a 49-spare pool past the 2× cap (11.1 and 13.3
points held to the cap). Reconfigurations, recovery time, and the power needed
per unit of training output fall. Lock-loss events rise 2% [composed].
and the reconfiguration factor adds the remaining 1.0, since
the thermal factor barely moves. Credited the other way round,
the two factors add 0.9. The availability share is provisioning:
it comes from the spare lasers that the coverage bound sizes,

1) A Correlated-Factor Composition: The multiplicative
model treats availability and thermal loss as independent,
but a shared cause could move both. The coupled model
assumes that one thermal event drives both the lock-loss stalls
(ThermaLead’s domain) and the correlation ρ (LightReserve’s),
so it moves both factors through the latent variable Θ of
Theorem 1. Multiplying the two means gives an expected
value and understates the tail, where both factors fail together.
The coupled model draws Θ ∼Beta(a, b) for each window.
Given the draw, the failures among the full stack’s lasers are
binomial at that level, so the pool either covers every one of
them or runs out. A window that runs out counts as lost, as the
coverage reading assumes. The thermal loss share is the full
stack’s share scaled by Θ/λ. Coverage and thermal loss thus
keep their stated means, and the model reports the distribution
of the goodput each window realizes.
The means agree: 76.5% under the coupled model and for
the independent point estimate. The coupling changes the tail
(Fig. 13). Goodput at the fifth percentile is 67.8%, and at
the first percentile it is 59.7%. A cluster provisioned to the
mean therefore misses its plan by 8.7 points or more in one
window out of twenty, and by 16.8 points or more in one out
of a hundred. This spread comes from the ρ of Theorem 1,
and the decorrelation that raises the ceiling also tightens the
spread. None of the per-component guarantees composes into
a worst-case bound on effective cluster goodput, but part of
the tail can be proved (Section V-V-E).
The stack is worth more under worse conditions. At 50 FIT
the four-laser reserve covers 99.974% of 90-day windows
and 99.896% of one-year windows. The 90-day figure already
exceeds the 99.9% target, so availability is held at that value.

Correlated-factor composition. Histogram of composed goodput,

and thermal loss together. Vertical lines mark the mean (76.5%), the fifth

plotted range fall 0.1% of windows, most of them windows whose failures

With the thermal and reconfiguration factors at their simulated
values, the composed gain falls to about 1.0 point, or 1.3%
relative, all of it from the reconfiguration factor. As the failure
rate rises at ρ = 0.15, the baseline’s goodput drops sharply
while the stack, its pool sized to 99.9% coverage, holds, and
the gap between them widens to 41 points at a failure rate of
0.18 per window (Fig. 14). At that rate the target takes 116
spares, far past the 2× cap; held to the cap, the stack keeps
73.2% against the baseline’s 35.1%, a gap of 38 points.
E. What Can Be Proved About the Goodput Tail
Section V-V-D reported a fifth-percentile goodput of 67.8%,
obtained by sampling the common driver Θ. A sampled
percentile is a simulation output: run the simulation differently
and the number moves. The systematic part of goodput, the
part Θ moves, has quantiles in closed form, so that part of the
