Fig. 15. Quantile transport. Closed-form quantile of the correlation-driven part
of goodput, G(Θ) of the coupled model in Section V-V-D, against the tail
percentile p, in percent. The dashed curve is the ρ = 0.15 operating point and
the solid curve the same pool after decorrelation to ρ = 0.03. Decorrelation
lifts the lower tail, including the fifth percentile; the curves cross near p = 22,
above which the more correlated pool sits higher [derived].
tail can be reasoned about as well as observed. The mechanism
is the standard monotone transport of quantiles.
Proposition 1 (Quantile transport). Let G be the systematic part
of the composed goodput, a strictly decreasing function of the
single driver Θ ∼Beta(a, b); the realized goodput is G plus
the conditional binomial variation of failures given Θ. Then,
for any p, the p-quantile of G is Qp(G) = G
␀F −1
Θ (1 −p)

.
For p below a threshold p∗that depends on λ and ρ and that
we locate numerically, ∂Qp/∂ρ < 0, so decorrelation lifts that
part of the tail.
Proof sketch. The identity is monotone transport of quantiles:
a strictly decreasing map sends the (1 −p)-quantile of its
input to the p-quantile of its output. The sign follows because,
for p < p∗, raising ρ moves the (1 −p)-quantile of Θ up,
which lowers G there; p∗is where that quantile stops rising
with ρ, which we locate numerically. We checked the identity


--- Page 17 ---
17
numerically, comparing empirical quantiles of four million
Monte Carlo draws of G(Θ) against the closed form, and the
two agree to within 2 × 10−4 at the reported percentiles.
Located numerically at λ = 0.05, p∗falls from the 31st
percentile at ρ = 0.03 to the 15th at ρ = 0.15 and the 8th at
ρ = 0.35, so it covers the fifth percentile across the plausible
band.
Fig. 15 plots this closed form. Realized goodput varies
further: the conditional binomial spread of failures given Θ
widens its distribution in both directions. Here G is the goodput
expected at a given Θ, a mean and not a minimum. In the
coupled model of Section V-V-D, a window’s realized goodput
sits slightly above G when its spares cover every failure. It
falls to zero in the 0.1% of windows where they run out, so
Qp(G) is no floor under realized goodput. At the percentiles
reported there the two agree to within 0.02 points: at p = 5 the
closed form gives the 67.8% sampled there. Turning Qp(G)
into a floor under realized goodput would require bounding the
conditional binomial spread as well, which we do not attempt
here.
F. Simulation Methodology and Reproducibility
The simulated and composed results in this and the preceding
sections come from a calibrated simulation stack written in
Python with NumPy and SciPy and run with fixed seeds; the
derived results are closed-form evaluations. None of them is
a hardware measurement. Each figure caption carries a prove-
nance tag: [derived] for closed-form evaluation, [composed] for
results composed arithmetically from the component outputs,
such as goodput and recovery time, [schematic] for architecture
drawings, and [synth; pnr; verified] for the synthesis, place-and-
route, and verification outputs reproduced in Section VI. Some
captions combine or qualify these base tags, as in [derived;
stated cost model], [synth; pnr], and [structure matches the
synthesized sources].
The configuration of each component follows, for repro-
duction; Section IV reports the results. LightReserve runs
Algorithm 1. The 32-channel calibration uses independent
failures at λ = 0.05, 0.10, and 0.20 with a 99% coverage
target, and a correlated case at λ = 0.05 and ρ = 0.15 with
targets of 99%, 99.9%, and 99.999%. FoldFit is simulated on
block-structured MoE demand, dense within each expert block
of 8 engines and sparse across blocks, on 8 channels at 8 to
128 engines. The simulation binary-searches the deadline and,
at each candidate, places the jobs longest first on a channel that
already holds the job’s expert block when one has room, and
otherwise on the least-loaded channel with room. It omits the
port condition, and with it the alignment step, so makespans
are measured against the larger of the largest demand and the
average load, which they meet from 64 engines up. ThermaLead
runs on the heat-cycle trace of Section IV-IV-C: over 30 seeds
the simulation counts lock-loss events per 2000 control steps
for ThermaLead, its gated variant, the dither lock, and an
oracle; it also sweeps the share of steps that carry a noise
burst from 30% down to none. TriageGuard is configured as
in Section IV-IV-D.
A reproducibility bundle accompanies the paper. It holds
the register-transfer sources, testbenches, proofs, build scripts,
and 130 nm layout flow behind Section VI; the component
simulator behind the results of Section IV, with the ThermaLead
baseline and gate studies and the abrupt-transient sweep of
Section VII-VII-D; the composite model, which reads the sim-
ulator’s output, behind the goodput, recovery-time, and capital
figures; the cross-workload simulations of Section VII-VII-C;
and the scripts that evaluate the closed-form results and draw
the figures.
VI. HARDWARE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE CONTROL
PLANE
Halley’s fallback to reactive control, which overrules a
forecast that is stale or unsure, needs a circuit to enforce
it. We implemented the two safety-critical parts of Halley
as one design for a Lattice iCE40UP5K [72], a small field-
programmable gate array (FPGA). The first is the fail-safe
watchdog, which enforces the fallback rule of Section IV:
cycle by cycle, it decides whether the predictive or the reactive
command reaches the actuator. The second is ThermaLead’s
local thermal servo, which drives the per-ring heaters and
is the only one of the four controllers that closes a loop at
hardware speed. LightReserve, FoldFit, and TriageGuard decide
on slower time scales: LightReserve sizes a pool when it is
provisioned or restocked, FoldFit computes a schedule for each
demand matrix, and TriageGuard ranks a pool’s modules from
their telemetry. A supervisory processor, such as the supervisory
host of Section VI-VI-C, can run all three in software, so none
of them needs dedicated logic. All four need telemetry and
actuation that published laser and switch interfaces provide
only in part (Section VII-VII-B), which is why the fallback is
the part of Halley that can be built and measured today.
The design was synthesized, placed and routed, and formally
verified with an open toolchain pinned to fixed versions: Icarus
Verilog 12.0 [73], Yosys 0.33 [74], nextpnr 0.6 [75], and the
icetime timing analyzer of Project IceStorm. The method is
test-driven [76], with an executable specification written before
the circuit. Every resource figure below regenerates exactly
from the released register-transfer sources. The timing figures
are the recorded results for each placement seed; a rebuild
can land at different frequencies on a given seed, and in our
independent rebuild of the core, the servo, the eight-instance
layout, and the ECP5 port, every seed we rebuilt still closed
timing.
A. Circuit Design
The safety core is one circuit with two halves that share
a clock and a reset. The first half is the watchdog of
Fig. 16, module watchdog_bypass. It lets the predic-
tive path drive the actuator only while the predictor keeps
answering and reports confidence. A windowed counter
restarts on each predictive_kick from the predictor
and otherwise counts up until it saturates at the 1,000-cycle
timeout, which a magnitude comparator detects. A registered
using_predictive flag is set when the counter is in
window and predictive_confidence_ok is high, and a

stage enables

Fig. 17. The ThermaLead local servo. The five numbered blocks are the pipeline stages of a multiplier-free proportional-integral law, from temperature error
to heater duty cycle. A label ≫n means an arithmetic shift right by n bits, which applies a gain without a multiplier. The strip below is the 256-cycle
pulse-width-modulation generator, which drives the per-ring heater and, once per period, launches the stage enables that step one update through the pipeline
[structure matches the synthesized sources].
second register raises watchdog_fault one cycle after the
window closes. The flag is the select of an output multiplexer
that holds no state of its own, and reset and power-up clear
it, so the reactive path is chosen unless the flag is set. A
crash, hang, low-confidence signal, or reset therefore parks the
actuator on the reactive path, which is always live, within at
most one trust window, 20 µs at the 50 MHz target clock, plus
one clock after the last kick, 20.02 µs in all. After a fresh kick,
the predictive path is restored within two clock cycles.
The second half is ThermaLead’s local loop, module
thermal_pi (Fig. 17), which turns a measured temperature
error into heater drive. Five pipeline stages compute error,
accumulate, clamp, control, and duty. Together they implement
a proportional-integral law whose two gains are arithmetic
shifts, one bit for the proportional gain and five for the integral
gain. The law therefore needs no multiplier, and it maps onto
look-up tables (LUTs) and carry cells instead of a dedicated
digital-signal-processing multiplier. The accumulator, clamped
to [0, 8191], is the only state carried from one update to the
next. The control sum is clamped to [0, 255] and registered
as the duty. A separate free-running 8-bit generator holds
pwm_out high while its counter sits below that duty, and that
signal drives the per-ring heater. The law updates once per
256-cycle pulse-width period, 5.12 µs at 50 MHz, so the five-
cycle pipeline latency is negligible against that period, and the
duty stream is bit-identical to a single-cycle implementation
of the same law. At that rate the heater drive does not limit
ThermaLead’s control step; the heater’s thermal response does
(see the closed-loop sweep below).
B. Chip Design
Table IV gives the toolchain results. The watchdog synthe-
sizes to 36 LUTs and the servo to 97, and the combined core
is exactly their sum, 133 LUTs, so either half can be budgeted
on its own. Counted at synthesis for the core alone, the 133
LUTs are 2.52% of the device’s 5,280.
Under nextpnr, timing closes on every placement seed. Placed
and routed behind the on-chip serial test harness, the combined
core closes at 68.97–74.69 MHz across ten seeds, a worst-
case margin of 38% over the target. The independent icetime

AND ROUTING FROM NEXTPNR ACROSS 10 SEEDS (THE WATCHDOG ALONE
ACROSS 3) AGAINST A 50 MHZ TARGET. FFS ARE FLIP-FLOPS, AND fmax IS

analyzer puts the combined core at 71.33–74.79 MHz on the
same placements, so both models clear the target on every
seed.
The core is paired with a production-grade sensor path on
a mode-zero serial-peripheral-interface (SPI) link. With that
path the design comes to 161 LUTs and closes on 10 of 10
seeds under both models. The same sources also port to a
second FPGA, a Lattice ECP5-25, where they close at 196.97–
211.91 MHz across three seeds, so the result is not tied to one
device. Unchanged, the core and its serial test harness also
lay out with LibreLane 3.0.14 as a 142 by 153 µm SkyWater
130 nm block, 0.022 mm2, with 128 flip-flops, the core’s 90
and the harness’s 38, among 995 standard cells besides fill
(Fig. 18b). The block meets 50 MHz at all nine signoff corners,
with 11.0 ns of worst-case setup slack, and passes design-rule,
layout-versus-schematic, and antenna checks; it has not been
fabricated.
Beyond the tests, four machine proofs by temporal induction
in Yosys check the core, each for every input. Temporal
induction proves a property outright for a bounded run of cycles,
then proves that any two consecutive cycles satisfying it force
the next cycle to satisfy it too, so the property holds for every
cycle. The first proof checks the watchdog against a one-bit-
wider golden model, an independently written reference circuit.
The second proves the servo’s invariants: the accumulator stays
in [0, 8191], the integral and the duty change only on their stage
enables, and pwm_out equals the comparison of counter and
duty. The third checks the servo pipeline against the one-shot
control law. The fourth checks the whole core, watchdog and
servo together, against an independent specification core whose
clamps are written as comparisons. The first two start checking
after eight cycles of warm-up, and the last two check every
cycle from power-on. All four report success on the induction
step in the released logs, so the bypass path that the control
plane relies on is a proven property of the register-transfer
design.
The proofs show that the circuit computes the law it was
meant to compute. They do not show that the law is well
behaved once the loop is closed, so the servo was also run
in closed loop against a second-order thermal plant with
quantization, noise, and one period of sensor delay. Across a
gain-and-pole sweep, it converges at all 31 feasible corners,
settling in 0.2 to 3.7 ms, and re-settles after a mid-run thermal
step in all 27 corners where one was injected. The one infeasible
corner asks for 500 counts at 0.6 times the nominal gain, more
than the 480 the plant reaches at full duty, and there the servo
correctly holds the duty at 255 and the integral at its cap. Its
phase and gain margins stay at or above 22.5° and 14.9 dB
across the sweep, and an independent recomputation confirms
them. The swept plant time constants include the 30.9 µs and
0.71 ms of a measured microring heater [77] and the 13.8 µs
of a metal microheater [78]; doped-silicon microheaters, at
0.98 µs [78], are faster than the sweep covers.
C. Packaging
The fallback can be built from catalog silicon with an
ordinary pinout: the iCE40UP5K in the 48-pad SG48 package.
The interface brought out to the package is deliberately
narrow (Fig. 18). A deployed part would carry setpoints and
telemetry to the supervisory host one level above this device
over a management bus such as I2C, in place of the two-pin
serial test port, and the wide data buses stay on chip behind that
serial test harness. Placed together with the harness, the design
occupies 202 of the 5,280 logic cells, or 3.83%, against the
2.52% that synthesis counts for the core alone. To test whether
one device can serve several thermal domains, we placed and
routed eight instances of the core without the shared telemetry
bus that would report them to the supervisory host. They occupy
1,417 of the 5,280 logic cells (26.8%) and close timing on
all six seeds under both models, at 55.25–58.59 MHz under
nextpnr and 55.91–58.92 MHz under icetime; the bus itself
has not been placed.
Both safety-critical circuits are placed and routed for a
shipping part, close timing under the place-and-route tool
on every seed, and use very little area, and the bypass is
a proven property of their register-transfer design, so the
fallback path can be built. Whether Halley then delivers
the reliability outcome still depends on the unmeasured
correlation ρ of Section III, which only the field measurement
of Section VII-VII-E would settle.
VII. DISCUSSION
A. Impact on Capital and Power Costs
The goodput gain of Section V-V-D is an upper bound
on the useful compute, and so the capital, that Halley frees.
The coverage reading multiplies the useful compute the same
hardware delivers by up to 1.17, a 17.3% rise, and the lit-
share reading by up to 1.03. Both factors hold only if fabric
stall is the sole recoverable loss, and it is not. Model FLOPs
utilization (MFU), the share of peak arithmetic that a training
run keeps busy, also counts compute, memory, pipeline-bubble,
and data-loading losses that the control plane never touches.
The 65.2% goodput here and the 38–43% MFU that Llama 3
reported therefore do not conflict.
At that bound, the gain cuts the accelerators, capital, and
provisioned power needed for a given training output by up to
14.7%, or 3.3% on the lit-share reading, for a fixed rack design
and power-smoothing scheme. Energy falls by less, because
accelerators waiting at a barrier draw less than full power [23].
Where power and local approval limit new AI data centers
(Section I), the gain becomes more training from existing sites
instead of a saving. It is a one-time factor on top of the 30
to 40% yearly improvement in accelerator performance per


--- Page 20 ---
20
logic array
5,280 cells
placed design
202 cells, 3.83%
Fig. 18. The device, the placement, and the pins, in the iCE40 and 130 nm
builds. (a) Inside the 48-pad SG48 package of the Lattice iCE40UP5K, the
inner square is the logic array, and the filled square, drawn to scale by area,
is the placed design: 202 logic cells including the serial test harness. Pad
positions and the design’s place in the array are schematic [synth; pnr]. (b)
The signed-off SkyWater 130 nm layout, drawn from its GDS: cells light blue,
the 128 flip-flops darker, pins as laid out [synth; pnr; verified].
watt [14], not a substitute for it. At 50 FIT the same arithmetic
starts from the 1.3% composed gain instead, and these capital
and power figures fall with it.
A control plane can address only the fabric’s share of
recoverable stall, the attribution fraction. Scaled by it, the
coverage reading’s 17.3% rise becomes 13.0%, 8.6%, and 5.8%
at three-quarters, half, and a third, and the lit-share reading’s
rise becomes 2.5%, 1.7%, and 1.1%. Llama 3 gives the fraction
a scale. A tenth of its 419 unexpected interruptions were traced
to network switches, cables, and interface cards [23], which
would put the gain near 1.7% on the coverage reading and 0.3%
on the lit-share reading. That breakdown counts interruptions,
not stalled time, so it gives a scale rather than a value, and this
work does not measure the fraction for a co-packaged fabric.
B. Addressing Practical System Losses
The results bear on four problems that operators pay for
today and that deployed systems leave open.
The first is time lost at the synchronization barrier in
hyperscale pretraining. Llama 3 held effective training time
above 90% through its 419 interruptions [23]. Laser-pool
exhaustion would add to that loss on a co-packaged fabric,
and within a budget cap Theorem 1 shows that more spares
alone cannot remove it. Decorrelation with fast recovery is
the alternative, and each point of availability recovers training
time in proportion to the attribution fraction.
The second is the tail-latency objective of MoE inference.
Generating a token runs the same all-to-all exchange as training;
that exchange takes 30–40% of iteration time in DeepSeek-V3
training on H100 before overlap with computation and under
5% after [22]. If decoding falls in the same range, FoldFit’s
11/9 bound caps the worst-case inflation of an iteration, under
its stated conditions, at 6.7–8.9% before switching delay and
with circuits held across steps, or at about 1% once the
exchange is overlapped.
The third is capacity planning before ρ is measured. Ob-
servation 2 shows that decorrelating first is the cheaper path
across the plausible band, and the coupled model plans against
the goodput tail that the independent model hides.
The fourth is the control interface. The algorithms are
cheap and step aside on a flagged forecast, so apart from
ThermaLead’s forecast (Section VII-VII-D) the obstacle to
deployment is an interface that exists only in part. External
laser modules report per-lane bias, power, and alarms and accept
per-lane enable [79], and commercial optical circuit switches
expose NETCONF and RESTCONF control [80]. Neither the
OIF management framework for co-packaged engines nor the
ELSFP interface, however, defines per-ring temperature or lock
state [79], [81]. One change would unblock both deployment
and the field measurement of ρ (Section VII-VII-E): a published
interface exposing per-laser health and failure timestamps, per-
ring temperature and lock state, and switch reconfiguration
hooks on the management interface the packages already carry.
C. Impact on Inference, Post-Training, and RL Traffic
Halley was developed for training, where the failure data
of Section II show the need. The same fabric now carries
inference and RL as well, but of the four components only
FoldFit carries a guarantee that transfers cleanly.
FoldFit transfers: MoE decoding runs the same all-to-all
expert dispatch on its critical path when experts are spread
across the fabric. Serving that disaggregates attention from the
experts sends M-to-N traffic instead [82]. On inference-shaped
demand, across expert-parallel degrees from 8 to 128 and
packed without the port condition, the schedule stays within
1% of the classical lower bound and never exceeds 11/9, so
the same cap on worst-case iteration inflation, before switching
delay, applies across that sweep. RL post-training inherits the
result through rollout, which is inference and takes from half
to over 90% of the step in reported systems [83]–[85]; by
Amdahl’s law, a hypothetical 10% rollout speed-up would
be roughly a 5 to 9% step speed-up. Weight synchronization
between phases is a separate load: under 1.6 s for a 72B model
inside one cluster, against rollouts of hundreds to thousands
of seconds [86], but enough to stall rollouts at terabyte scale,
especially across data centers [87].
Availability and thermal are training-first: Reported
machine failures run about 13.6× lower per thousand machines
per week for an inference service than for pretraining at scale,
2.2 against 30 [88]. If the per-laser rate fell by the same
factor, the same coverage bound would put a fixed four-laser


--- Page 21 ---
21
reserve at 99.1% availability, against 86.3% at the stress training
rate. The machinery pays off most where failures are frequent
and correlated, so we claim no per-component inference win
for LightReserve, ThermaLead, or TriageGuard. The case is
strongest on the largest jobs, since mean time to failure falls as
the GPU count rises [27]; at platform scale, ByteDance logged
38,236 explicit and 5,948 implicit failures across 778,135
training jobs in three months [89].
Disaggregated serving also moves the key-value cache from
prefill to decode over the fabric [90], [91], a load that grows
with context. No component removes it, and we claim no
guarantee for it.
D. Limitations and Open Problems
The fallback rule of Section IV covers the cases it can
detect: on a stale, low-confidence, or late signal, the component
bypasses itself. It does not catch a confident but wrong forecast,
on which a controller can reconfigure the fabric more often than
it should. Gating reconfiguration on confidence and feasibility
curbs that churn without eliminating it, and a formal bound
on the harm is left to future work. Acting also costs compute
for the predictions and energy for the heaters, and spoofed
telemetry could force a mis-reconfiguration, so the control
interface has to be hardened.
Every numerical result outside Section VI is a calibrated
simulation or a closed-form evaluation, and those of Section VI
are synthesis, place-and-route, signoff, and proof outputs, which
settle the logic and its static timing but leave the process and
interfaces to fabrication; none is a measurement on hardware.
The two loss shares of the goodput model are assumptions,
and most of the stress-point gain comes from provisioning the
spare lasers that the coverage bound sizes (Section V-V-D).
Six limits bound the claims.
First, the failure inputs are assumed: the correlation ρ, on
which both the sparing result and the ceiling depend, and the
per-laser failure rate, for which we found no published field
value for the lasers inside external laser modules. The headline
figures use the stress setting λ = 0.05 per window, and 99.999%
stays out of reach inside the 2× cap of the 32-channel pool
only while λ exceeds about 2.4 × 10−4 (Table II). We anchor
ρ in the common-cause beta factors of Section III-III-B but
cannot yet calibrate it to field data for these laser form factors,
so the recommendation rests on the sweep of Observation 2.
Second, of the three conditions that carry FoldFit’s 11/9
guarantee onto a switch (Section IV-IV-B), two hold by
construction here. The third, realizing the packing as port-
disjoint configurations, is exact only when a demand may be
split at a configuration boundary and resumed later, and a proof
for demands that must each run on one uninterrupted circuit
is open. The guarantee also covers dwell time only, not the
switching delay of each reconfiguration.
Third, ThermaLead’s moving-average forecast does slightly
worse than the dither lock on the stress trace of Section IV-IV-C,
and in the released sweep its deficit grows to 49–67% when
the heat cycle’s phase jumps randomly every 16 steps or more
often, and to 17% under random temperature steps of 1 °C
standard deviation every 4 steps. Gated, both deficits stay
within 4.3%, an empirical limit, not a proof. A deployable
ThermaLead needs a forecast matched to the drift and aware
of regime changes. Comparisons with the fastest reactive loops
now reported [56] and with heater pre-driving from kernel
launches [57] remain open, since both need the control step in
seconds, which the per-step analysis leaves free.
Fourth, several external anchors are vendor-reported or
forward-looking, and each is hedged where it appears. Fifth,
Proposition 1 covers only the correlation-driven part of goodput,
and Section V-V-E states what a genuine floor under realized
goodput would also require. Sixth, the composed goodput turns
on what a spare shortfall costs a real job, and the two readings
of Section V-V-D are cases, not bounds.
E. The Measurement That Turns the Bound into a Forecast
Theorem 1 bounds availability in terms of ρ, so a fleet-
scale measurement of that correlation would pin down the
value on which the bound depends, and the measurement
needs only instrumentation. Log the failure timestamp of every
laser across many identical pools, count how many lasers fail
together in each restock window, and estimate ρ from how
far that count is over-dispersed, that is, how much more it
varies than the independent-binomial expectation. Random-
effects lifetime models, which already estimate location-driven
correlation from GPU fleet failure data [92], offer one way
to do it. Correlated failures are rare, so a credible estimate
needs exposure on the order of thousands of pool-years, from
a hyperscaler instrumenting its own packages or a vendor
publishing co-failure statistics. Two choices sharpen the result.
Logging the candidate shared causes lets ρ be attributed to a
mechanism. The full per-window distribution should also be
reported, because Part (2) of Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 show
that coverage and the goodput tail depend on the tail of Θ, not
only on its variance. Until such data exists, ρ = 0.15 should be
read as a prior, and the design should rest on the full ρ-sweep.
Cheaper measurements would narrow other unmeasured inputs:
one instrumented package would ground the two composition
loss shares, and one real job would establish both the fabric’s
share of recoverable stall and what a spare shortfall costs it.
VIII. CONCLUSIONS
This paper argues that each of the four optical layers can
be run a step ahead of failure. Halley puts one predictive
controller over each of them, though ThermaLead’s simple
forecast paid off mainly on smoother drift; its gate kept it near
the dither lock elsewhere. Each controller steps aside when its
forecast is flagged stale or unsure, so for such a forecast the
worst case is the reactive system it replaces; a confident but
wrong forecast has no such floor yet (Section VII-VII-D).
One theorem shapes the design: correlated laser failures
put a ceiling on the coverage a large pool can reach within
a deployable budget cap. For a 32-channel pool at ρ = 0.15,
99.999% stays out of reach within the 2× cap whenever a
laser’s failure probability per restock window exceeds about
2.4 × 10−4, as it does for a laser at the 50 FIT source target
restocked once a year. Between that target and the stress level,
correlation raises the spares that 99.999% takes more than


--- Page 22 ---
22
tenfold. That target is then reached by decorrelating the pool
first and sizing the spares against the correlation that remains.
Under the stated cost model, that path costs $44,100 at the
stress operating point against $234,000 for the pure-spares
alternative, a 5.3× saving, and it stays the cheaper of the two
across the whole plausible band of ρ, which the field has not
yet measured.
Composed from the simulated components, effective cluster
goodput at the stress operating point rose 11.3 points on the
coverage reading and 2.2 points on the lit-share reading. Most
of the first figure comes from the larger spare pool, and holding
it to the 2× cap leaves 11.1 points. The margin over today’s
reactive stack is narrowest under mild conditions, about 1.3%
in relative terms at 50 FIT. How much of that gain a real job
would keep depends on the fabric’s share of recoverable stall,
which this work did not measure. The part of the gain that a
job keeps reduces the accelerators and megawatts its training
needs, by up to 3.3–14.7% at the stress operating point. That
much data center capacity need not be built. The fallback that
early action relies on is synthesized, placed and routed for a
shipping FPGA and passes signoff as a 130 nm layout, and
its combined core is machine-proven to match an independent
specification core on every cycle.
An operator should size the pool from a measured failure
rate and a measured correlation, spend the next dollar on
separating the lasers before buying more of them, and plan
capacity against a bad window such as the fifth percentile.
Further research can help realize a deployed system. What
remains open, ThermaLead’s forecast and the theory, is stated
in Section VII-VII-D. Running these controllers on real optics
needs the parts of the telemetry and actuation interface
that the optics vendors have not yet published, chiefly per-
ring temperature and lock state. Estimating ρ across a fleet
needs only enough pools instrumented for long enough. This
measurement would turn the ceiling proved here from a bound
conditioned on an assumed correlation into a forecast.
